zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510 (supplied page subset), CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Used for lexical identification after reading the scan, not as the authority for diplomatic spelling or typography. Lexical references are paraphrased in the English comments; the transcription was read independently from this scan.

lines.note: The inherited fragment ends a definition concerning royal dignity; gosokui de gozaru refers to accession or enthronement. The absent beginning is not supplied, and this leaf is not forced to continue f0442's unrelated catchword.
Sokuji and sokujini mean immediately, matching Logo. Sunauachino corrects Sanauachino and supplies the native explanatory phrase; l introduces the alternative form.
Sokujoozuge is explained literally with the feet above and the head below. Xi- begins xitani across the break; the caron and doubled z are preserved.

runs.text: De pees pera cima, & de cabeça pera

lines.note: Completes shita ni and translates the inverted position, feet upward and head downward. The Portuguese pees and pera are retained as printed.
Completes the literal inversion and paraphrases it as entirely the wrong way round. The terminal upright S. is the dictionary's written-register label, not part of the italic gloss.
Sokumet is glossed as destruction, with sunawachi messuru as the Japanese explanation. The final t and printed s-types are retained without adding a modern vowel ending.
Sokunan is equated with onoko and glossed as a male or man. The initial V in Vonoco is a historical spelling, not a voiced consonant to normalize.
Sokusanhengi is described as islands near a larger realm. The printed f corresponds to the historical h-row spelling; the geographical explanation continues below.
Completes the definition as islands near a great kingdom or the mainland. No particular archipelago is named in the printed gloss.
Sokutaku is equated with zasshoo and denotes a present or gift. Vi- begins vinho, one example of such a gift.
Completes vinho and adds foodstuffs as suitable gifts. This continuation explains the preceding noun, not a new entry.
The verb sokutai concerns dressing or adorning oneself. Its printed principal forms use carons and remain distinct from the following nominal entry.
The clothing and attire are clean and suitable. This completes the verbal definition of dressing appropriately.
The noun sokutai denotes the adornment or appearance of clothing. The repeated headword starts an example rather than a second entry on this row.
Sokutai kekkoo ni gozatta says that the attire was splendid. The Portuguese refers to the ornament and lustre of the clothing, completed below.
Completes the statement that the appearance of the attire was excellent. The double l in excellente remains as printed.

runs.text: Vaſo como tina que ſerue de latrinas.

lines.note: Sokutsuu denotes a tub-like vessel used as a privy. The scan supports tç rather than eç and a caron over the final u; these correct the malformed Socueçù hint.

runs.text: Socuxit. Sumiyacani taxi. i, Monono fayai

lines.note: Sokushit is explained as quickness or speed. The first explanatory phrase visibly appears to end in taxi, with a, although the sense invites comparison with an adjective for swift. That chosen reading is retained rather than emended; mono no hayai koto continues below.
Completes mono no hayai koto and translates it as something swift and light or nimble. The final t in the headword is a historical checked coda.

runs.text: Certa toada, ou modo de voz cõ que

lines.note: Sokushoo names a particular chant or vocal manner. Its Portuguese relative clause continues to identify the performers and the poems.

runs.text: os Chinas cantão huns verſos q̃ chamão

lines.note: The Chinese sing verses called shi. Xi is a Japanese reading-name embedded in Portuguese and is printed upright; Chinas remains the Portuguese designation.
Sodachi, sodatsu, sodatta concerns being nourished or growing up. The intransitive meaning contrasts with the later sodate entry.

runs.text: Homem que tem por officio acudir às

lines.note: Soodai denotes someone charged with attending to communal needs. A faint circumflex is read over o; the Portuguese office-description continues below.

runs.text: neceßidades commũas de toda a cidade, ou

lines.note: These are the shared needs of the whole city or settlement. Commũas retains the printed nasal abbreviation rather than modern spelling.

Completes the office-holder's remit with the settlement or community. The very weak a before ç is recovered as pouoação after enlargement and comparison with its immediate letter shapes; this remains a nonblocking damaged-letter reading.
Soodaiku is the chief carpenter or master of works. The clear circumflex in the headword is preserved, while the second Portuguese alternative continues below.
Completes mestre das obras, the master responsible for the building works. This is not a separate occupational entry.

Soodan is consultation, explained by ai kataru, speaking together. Conſulta corrects Conſila. The worn right-hand stroke above o is provisionally read as a caron; the supplied NINJAL lexical aid supports the identification but does not establish this copy's accent.
Sodate is the transitive verb for rearing or sustaining. The comma after the headword and cedilla in tçuru are visible and correct the draft's punctuation and tcuru.
Hito wo torisodatsuru means bringing someone up. The Portuguese alguẽ keeps its abbreviation tilde and is followed by another phrasing below.
The alternative is bringing someone to adulthood; homem corrects bomem. Ki wo uye sodatsuru then extends the verb to planting and nurturing trees.
The trees are planted and raised. The gloss confirms that sodate can concern plants as well as people.
Sode means sleeves. Sode wo nurasu, wetting one's sleeves, introduces an expression for weeping; Deſ- starts the Portuguese equivalent.
Completes desfazer-se em lágrimas, dissolving into tears. Sode ga nururu gives the intransitive counterpart, the sleeves becoming wet.
Idem gives the same weeping sense to wet sleeves. Sode wo shiboru, wringing the sleeves, denotes crying greatly.
Sode wo tsuranuru, lining up sleeves, describes being together with many people. The communal setting is completed on the next row.

runs.text: junta, ou em companhia de muitos.

lines.note: Completes the explanation as being gathered together or in the company of many. The sleeve expression is social rather than a sewing instruction.

runs.text: Veſtido de pelles como coura que ſe

lines.note: Sodeboso denotes a skin or fur outer garment compared with a leather jerkin. The damaged vowel is read as o, not the draft's a; the clothing description supports this lexical identification.
The garment is worn on top of other clothing. The scan supplies the t in veſte that the draft omitted.
Sodegaki is equated with hashigaki, an additional or repeated note in a letter. Repetição corrects Repeuição; the gloss describes its placement below.

runs.text: faz no principio da carta de letra mais miuda.

lines.note: The note is written at the beginning of the letter in smaller script. Miuda corrects miuſa; the account preserves the dictionary's stated position rather than imposing a modern convention.
Sodegoi means begging for alms. The scan clearly restores Sodegoi from Fodegui, and the same word begins the divided example.
Completes sodegoi wo suru, begging or soliciting alms. The short Japanese continuation keeps its own physical line and crop.
Sodeguchi is the opening of a sleeve. The Portuguese Boca corrects Bora and directly explains the guchi element.

Sooden is transmission or tradition, explained by passing something on. The faint accent is provisionally read as a caron, supported more clearly by the repeated word in the example; the supplied NINJAL aid independently identifies the headword.
The teaching passes from one person to another. Outro corrects outiro, and dai- begins daidai, successive generations, in the example.

Completes a statement that the teaching has been transmitted in this manner through generations. The repeated sǒden is visibly lowercase with a caron; Esta begins the Portuguese sentence continued in column 2.

zones.label: Printed page number
zones.note: The figures 224 are clear. The damaged adjacent mark is represented as the terminal full stop, with the small higher speck treated as stray ink rather than an additional punctuation point.

runs.text: dostrina vem desta maneira de muitas idades

lines.note: Continues Esta from the other column: the teaching has come down in this manner through many ages. The printed dostrina spelling is retained rather than modernized to doutrina.
Transmission by tradition completes the previous sentence. This is the end of the sooden example, not a fresh entry.
This sooden is an early rice field, equated with wasada. The agricultural homonym is separate from the preceding transmission entry despite the similar romanization.
The field is either sown early or among the first harvested. Sega here concerns reaping, not a different geographical feature.
Sodenashi is a doobuku or other sleeveless garment. Dôbucu is one complete embedded Japanese term, not a roman ô surrounded by Portuguese fragments; its whole-word typography is recorded together.
Sode no taki, literally the waterfall of the sleeves, is a poetic expression for tears. P. is the poetic-use label; Namida is the Japanese synonym, not an embedded Portuguese term.
Sode yuku mizzu is another poetic name for tears. The scan shows doubled z in mizzu, unlike the draft; La- begins the Portuguese Lagrimas below.
Completes Lagrimas, tears. The short continuation closes the poetic sleeve-and-water expression.
Soodoo denotes disturbance, explained by agitation and movement. The first circumflex and second caron are visibly different and are preserved independently.

runs.text: Curi ſôdǒni xite zajen mini ximazu.

lines.note: The saying describes kitchen commotion preventing meditation from sinking in. Curi corrects Ciri. The final letter of zajen is partly lost and is provisionally read as n with support from the meditation gloss; the first accent in ſôdǒni is a circumflex.
The Portuguese specifies bustle and activity in the kitchen. It confirms Curi as the kitchen term rather than an unrelated kiri reading.

runs.text: não ſe pode aduertir, ou entender na meditação.

lines.note: One cannot attend to or concentrate on meditation amid that commotion. This completes the explanatory translation rather than offering a separate doctrinal definition.
Kuni ga soodoo suru applies the disturbance sense to a realm. The printed joining of ſôdǒſuru is preserved without inserting a modern word boundary.
The realm is disturbed or experiences revolts. This completes the political example rather than the preceding kitchen saying.
A separate soodoo entry introduces a list of five Buddhist buildings or spaces. The list is Japanese example material, not Japanese words embedded in a Portuguese sentence.

runs.text: Cinco lugares, ou caſas eſtimadas ẽtre os bõzos

lines.note: The dictionary describes five valued places or buildings among Buddhist clergy. The abbreviated ẽtre and bõzos are retained without expansion.

runs.text: ſ. A caſa, ou mosteiro de Bonzos, a Igreja

lines.note: The explanatory ſ. introduces the list: a monastic residence, then the place compared with a church. These are the source's Portuguese analogies, not modern institutional equivalences.

runs.text: onde fazem os officios e ſe ajunta o pouo, capel

lines.note: The worship hall is where services are performed and people gather. Capel continues as capella on the next row, with no inferred hyphen added.

runs.text: la, ou oratorio õde poẽ o Fotoque, cozinha, &

lines.note: Completes capella and names an oratory housing a Buddhist image, then the kitchen. Fotoque is the embedded Japanese term; the source's Portuguese religious vocabulary is preserved.

runs.text: hũa caſa, ou portal de ſobrado õde estão muitos

lines.note: The final listed building is a raised or upper-storey gate-house containing many images. This continues the same architectural list.

runs.text: Idolos que dizẽ ſerem os diſcipulos do Fotoque.

lines.note: The images are said to represent disciples of the Buddha. Fotoque again occurs inside Portuguese; Idolos is the historical author's terminology rather than an editorial characterization.

runs.text: Sǒdǒ. Cuſano dǒ, i, ſoſǒna dǒ.

lines.note: Another soodoo is a grass-roofed or roughly made hall, explained by kusa no doo and sosoo na doo. These Japanese equivalents are not embedded Portuguese terms.
The hermitage is covered with straw or poorly made. The scan reads malfeita with f, correcting malſeita; this is a meaning-changing letter distinction.
Soofa is explained through sea and waves. The example begins crossing a vast distance at sea; the unpunctuated Vt is retained as printed.
Completes the Japanese example with wo shinogu, braving or traversing the sea. The Portuguese describes crossing great seas with hardship; tra- joins balho below.
Completes trabalho, the effort or hardship involved in the preceding sea crossing. This short continuation is a separate printed row.
Soofan is an early meal, glossed by hayai ii. The Portuguese says to dine early; its verbal phrasing does not require changing the Japanese noun.
Soheki is a poorly made wall, explained by orosoka na kabe. The Portuguese adjective feita is physically divided fei-/ta.
The wall is poorly made, old and dilapidated. The example pairs a poor wall with damaged windows or openings; the apparent break within deſmãchada is damaged impression, not a word space.

runs.text: Paredes, portas, ou janelas velhas, & desfeitas.

lines.note: Translates the paired example as old, broken walls, doors or windows. The broader Portuguese list explains the example rather than introducing additional Japanese entries.
Soohitsu, literally a fast brush, denotes a quick writer here. The initial is a capital S, correcting the draft's lowercase letter; the final printed t is preserved.
The adjectival form soohitsu na receives the same explanation as the preceding fast writer. Idem refers to that entry, not to the following one.
Soohoo means both sides or both parties. The scan has a capital S, not the draft's g, and a v-shaped mark over each o is transcribed as the caron used elsewhere for this vowel category.
Sogaku is superficial learning, explained by studying carelessly. The Portuguese begins a description of study of little substance, with pouco divided at the row end.

runs.text: co tomo, ou estudo, que hum fez com pouco

lines.note: Completes pouco tomo, study of little weight or importance, then restates it as study undertaken with little care. Hum is retained as historical Portuguese spelling.
Completes the description of inadequate care and diligence. The example begins sogaku na hito; cuidado has c rather than the draft's erroneous e.

runs.text: Homem imperfeito nas letras, ou que

lines.note: Hito completes the Japanese phrase for an imperfectly learned person. The Portuguese says a man deficient in learning, with an alternative explanation continuing below.
The alternative is someone who studies in this careless manner. The row completes the sogaku example and its explanation.
Soogan means the two eyes together, explained by paired eyes and the synonym ryoogan. The visible stop after manaco is retained before i,; Am- joins bos below.
Completes ambos os olhos and gives an example of tears welling in both eyes. Nanda is the printed form and is not silently replaced by a modern equivalent.

runs.text: Estarem ambos os olhos arraſados ẽ lagrimas.

lines.note: The Portuguese describes both eyes brimming with tears. Arraſados is retained in this historical expression; the nasal abbreviation ẽ is visible.
Soogan, alternatively sookan, is a Buddhist clerical rank. The source prints the voiced and unvoiced forms separately, and Bon- continues as Bonzos.
Completes Bonzos, the Portuguese designation for Buddhist clergy in the preceding definition. This short suffix occupies its own physical row.
Soogedatsu is for all one's hair to stand on end. The abbreviated conjugational ending u and the printed spelling Arrepiarenſe are retained.
Soogeki is disorder or disturbance, explained through commotion and becoming disordered. The Portuguese gives the corresponding noun perturbação.
The example says that the country falls into disorder. Reino has n in the scan, not the draft's m; the Japanese example is not a term embedded inside the Portuguese sentence.
Soogetsu, identified with Shimotsuki, is the eleventh lunar month. The definition continues beyond this page; mes is not supplied with an unprinted full stop or completion.
